title: A first-term money map
description: Student money often arrives in lumps while spending flows weekly. A term map — income divided by weeks — turns the lump into a livable rhythm.

body.heading: Divide by the weeks, honestly
paragraphs: Add up everything you will receive this term: loans, grants, family help, job income you can count on. Divide by the number of weeks in the term. That weekly figure — not the impressive lump in your account in week one — is your real income.
Suppose the term brings $2,600 across thirteen weeks. That is $200 a week, from which rent and bills may already claim their share. Seeing the weekly truth early is the entire trick.

body.heading: Take the big costs off the top
paragraphs: Subtract the term's fixed costs first: rent, bills, travel passes, course materials. What remains is your weekly living money. Move the fixed-cost share somewhere it cannot be casually spent — a separate account or pot — the day the lump arrives.

Freshers' weeks and end-of-term celebrations are the two danger zones: one spends the term's money in a fortnight, the other arrives when the account is thinnest. A term map that expects both survives both.

body.heading: Review at half-term
paragraphs: Halfway through, compare the map with reality and adjust the weekly figure up or down honestly. A small correction at week six is painless; the same correction discovered in week twelve is not.

If the map shows the money will not stretch, act at half-term rather than at the end: more hours at work, a word with the student support office, or a honest conversation at home are all easier with weeks still in hand. Early honesty is the cheapest financial tool there is.

takeaway: Divide your term's income by its weeks, set the fixed costs aside the day the money lands, and re-check at half-term — lumpy income, weekly life, no surprises.
